I'll try to start this from a novice's perspective, as in the, I am dog, and have no clue what I'm trying to do.

So, you want to start reloading? Saving money (ahahahaha. More on this later), making awesomely wild and crazy loads (we both know you secretly want to stuff anything and everything that'll fit into a 12 gauge). But, you're rather attached to your hands, as most of us are, and you really want to keep them. So, we'll get to that next.

Firstly, reloading is taking your fired cases, cleaning them up (there's a few different methods), removing the spent primers, resizing your fired cases back to spec, then adding primer, powder, and bullet, then ending up with a finished product.
So, lets talk about reloading. I'm going to post some stuff, feel free to ask away.

First step: Cleaning. There's a few ways you can do this. To break it down to the most simplistic options, you can clean your cases before or after removing the primer (and/or resizing) and do it wet or dry. I personally prefer dry tumbling, which uses crushed walnut shells, some nu finish polish, and a vibrating tumblr. They cost ~100 bucks.

IF you're cheap or want to do it a different way, you can remove the primers, then clean in hot soapy water, then let them air dry or bake the cases in a NOT for food oven at like 150* or so.

Safety warning: Don't breathe the dust, don't get the liquid on your skin. Don't give yourself lead poisoning.

Step 1.5 or 2.0.

We need to remove the primers from your fired cases. Look at your case, see that ugly dimple on the primer? That means it's spent. Like condoms, primers are a one time use item. Just like condoms, if you go full crazy, you can reuse them, but just fucking buy 15k of them and never worry about it again.

So, there's two ways to pop the primer out. For the american style primers and brass that has one flash hole (if you look in the center of your case, there's one centered hole). Boxer vs berdan primers, photo. We want the boxer primed We'll discuss this more in depth later.

So, a depriming die is just a stick that pokes out the old primer. I prefer a depriming die that is also a resizing die, as it does two steps at once. It pushes out the old primer, while squeezing the brass case back down to size. Because, the brass has to be smaller then the chamber to fit into the chamber and when it fires, it expands to fill the chamber. A split second later, it springs back to a smaller size, but still larger then the original size. So, we need to squeeze it back down to size.

The best way to check your sizing afterwards, is to drop a deprimed and resized case into your barrel and see that it drops in nice and easy.

Step 3: Priming again. So, there's a few methods you can use. Hand priming with a hand priming tool, or using a on press tool. I prefer on press priming, for obvious reasons, even for my precision stuff. Fuck hand priming. Fuck that so hard.

Next, you need to identify the primer size. Small pistol, large pistol, magnum pistol, large rifle, small rifle, magnum primers.

You can get softer primers (good for ignition, good for accurate loads) or hard primers (good for duty loads, less sensitive loads, I prefer it in my competition loads).

How to prime you ask? You forcefully yet gently shove it in the hole, explodey side up. Just gently and firmly shove it into the hole. Make sure it's deep enough. Run your Mki mod 0 finger over the rim of the case, you want the primer to be level with or below the rim of the case.

Step four: Powder charge choosing.

First, decide on a powder, look at some manuals, and see what's common for your cartridge. AS a rule, larger cases like bulkier and slower powders (as far as pistols). Check your manuals.

Here's where it gets fun, we're going to talk about how to not blow your hands off.

Magnum primers cause a bit more vigorous of a burn, and increase FPS a little bit (useful for game loads) and also, psi.

Unless you buy a load sensor, you're never going to know the PSI, and reading brass is ... not an exact science, but it's the best we can do, without a chronograph. BUY A CHRONOGRAPH.

Lets talk about internal ballistics.

Pistols: You have a correlation between bullet weight, Case overall length, and powder charge. Keeping the bullet weight the same, the more powder you add, the faster and more PSI in the case (naturally). Adding a heavier bullet will increase the PSI inside the case as well (keeping the powder charge the same). Now, with Overall length, seating the bullet further into the case, increases pressure, as you shrink the volume of the case. Seating the bullet out farther decreases pressure by increasing volume.

RIFLE: Works the opposite way. Shoving the bullet into the case doesn't harm anything, and will decrease pressures. Seating the bullet long will increase pressure, because it'll start interacting with the rifling, and have less inertia to it when it meets the rifling. This is why for most accurate loads, you want JUST OFF the rifling, not into the rifling. You want that bullet to have some momentum.

Know what you're looking for, and decide on a powder charge per your bullet weight.

On brass and reloading. Remember that brass work hardens. The rapid increase of pressure fire forms the brass to your chamber. When you resize the brass you squeeze it down. This causes the brass to become harder and there for brittle causing cracking of the neck. You may want to anneal the brass prior to reloading. To anneal the brass stand the brass on its base in a pan of water. Using a propane torch heat the neck areas to a cherry red and then tip over into the water to rapidly cool it. Also for plinking ammo I recommend that you reload your ammo to the lower velocities. The high velocity reduces the life of the brass cartridge case. Also high velocities burn barrels. One of the gripes about the .220 swift and the .264 Winchester Magnum was that they were barrel burners. (Often life spans of only 1500 to 2000 rounds). How ever it was found that if you loaded them to much lower velocities they lasted 10,000 to 20,000 rounds. JD

Thank you! I was going to cover this in 'advanced reloading 101' especially on the trade off between brass life and reliability. I resize my brass down like a mofo so it'll load into any gun I own in that caliber.

Barrel burners don't usually eat the barrel, it's more eroding out the throat, necessitating setting back the barrel a half turn, due to heat and pressure erosion. Thank you JD for adding valuable knowledge to the conversation.

If you really want to have cheap bullets you might want to start lead casting. I cast lead projectiles for .30 cal. and .45 ACP. The 30 cal projectile is a gas checked 173 grain lead projectile loaded with 8 grains of Unique if I remember correctly. This rounds chronographs out at around 1100 fps and as the trajectory of a rock. Being soft lead it also doesn't ricochet. My lead I scrounge out of .22cal Rim fire ranges and melt into ingots. You can also buy lead shot (trap shooters buy this stuff) and melt down. The only addition equipment you will need is a lead pot, and bullet molds. Then there is the Lubrisizer that sizes the lead projectile down to proper size and places lubricating grease in the lands around the bullets. The Lubrisizer also places the brass gas check at the bottom of the bullet, My .45 Cal lead cast is a Elmer Keith designed semi Wad cutter that is pressure formed in a hydraulic press. This is an excellent round for target shooting. However you do get some lead fouling in the barrel. I always shoot some hard ball after lead to remove the lead in the bore. Lyman makes all the tools you need to get started in lead casting bullets.
Casting is a wonderful thing! Especially when you can get freeish lead. I don't cast currently, so I don't have any real experience to add about it, feel free to add more to the conversation though!
